title.es: Voz narrativa y punto de vista

es: Reconocer la voz narrativa (primera persona, tercera limitada u omnisciente) en fragmentos breves y justificarla con una pista.

teaching.en: I open the letter and my hands tremble, but I cannot say what my sister feels, because a first-person narrator only knows his or her own mind and sees events from a single vantage point.
teaching.es: Abro la carta y me tiemblan las manos, pero no puedo decir qué siente mi hermana, porque un narrador en primera persona solo conoce su propia mente y ve los hechos desde un único punto de vista.
teaching.explanationEs: El pronombre I es la pista de la primera persona: el narrador es un personaje y solo cuenta lo que vive y siente.
segments: I open the letter and my hands tremble, but I cannot say what my sister feels, because a
first-person narrator only knows his or her own mind and sees events from a single vantage point.
teaching.audioText: I open the letter and my hands tremble, but I cannot say what my sister feels, because a first-person narrator only knows his or her own mind and sees events from a single vantage point.

teaching.en: Mara opens the letter and wonders why her father has written after so many years, yet the narrator never steps inside his mind.
teaching.es: Mara abre la carta y se pregunta por qué ha escrito su padre después de tantos años, pero el narrador nunca entra en la mente de él.
teaching.explanationEs: Tercera persona limitada: el narrador sigue a Mara y solo conocemos sus pensamientos.
segments: Mara opens the letter and wonders why her father has written after
so many years, yet the narrator never steps inside his mind.
teaching.audioText: Mara opens the letter and wonders why her father has written after so many years, yet the narrator never steps inside his mind.

teaching.en: An omniscient narrator is privy to every character's thoughts, so the reader learns what Mara fears and what her father is hiding.
teaching.es: Un narrador omnisciente está al tanto de los pensamientos de todos los personajes, así que el lector sabe lo que teme Mara y lo que oculta su padre.
teaching.explanationEs: Omniscient: el narrador entra en varias mentes a la vez; be privy to significa estar al tanto de algo reservado.
segments: An omniscient narrator is privy to every character's thoughts, so the
reader learns what Mara fears and what her father is hiding.
teaching.audioText: An omniscient narrator is privy to every character's thoughts, so the reader learns what Mara fears and what her father is hiding.

teaching.en: A limited narrator shows one mind only, whereas an omniscient one moves freely between several minds and sometimes comments on events from a distance.
teaching.es: Un narrador limitado muestra una sola mente, mientras que uno omnisciente se mueve con libertad entre varias y a veces comenta los hechos desde lejos.
teaching.explanationEs: Limited y omniscient se distinguen por cuántas mentes abre el narrador; whereas contrasta los dos tipos.
segments: A limited narrator shows one mind only, whereas an omniscient one moves
freely between several minds and sometimes comments on events from a distance.
teaching.audioText: A limited narrator shows one mind only, whereas an omniscient one moves freely between several minds and sometimes comments on events from a distance.

teaching.en: An unreliable narrator may mislead you, so look for any clue that can reveal the gap between what he claims and what really happened.
teaching.es: Un narrador poco fiable puede engañarte, así que busca cualquier pista que revele la diferencia entre lo que afirma y lo que realmente ocurrió.
teaching.explanationEs: Unreliable describe a quien cuenta con sesgo o mentiras; mislead es inducir a error a quien lee.
segments: An unreliable narrator may mislead you, so look for any clue that
can reveal the gap between what he claims and what really happened.
teaching.audioText: An unreliable narrator may mislead you, so look for any clue that can reveal the gap between what he claims and what really happened.

teaching.en: The tone may be warm or detached, and that voice, more than the pronoun alone, tells you how much the narrator cares about the characters.
teaching.es: El tono puede ser cálido o distante, y esa voz, más que el pronombre por sí solo, te dice cuánto le importan los personajes al narrador.
teaching.explanationEs: La voz narrativa es el tono y la actitud de quien cuenta; detached significa sin implicación emocional.
segments: The tone may be warm or detached, and that voice, more than the
pronoun alone, tells you how much the narrator cares about the characters.
teaching.audioText: The tone may be warm or detached, and that voice, more than the pronoun alone, tells you how much the narrator cares about the characters.

prompt.es: Lee el fragmento. ¿Qué muestra que solo conocemos la mente de quien cuenta?

choices.text: The pronoun I is used, and the narrator cannot tell what the sister thinks.
The pronoun I is used, and the narrator reports what the sister secretly feels.
The pronoun I is avoided, and the narrator describes how the sister feels.

feedback.es: El narrador dice I y admite que no sabe si su hermana ya la leyó: solo accede a su propia mente.

hint.es: Busca el pronombre y comprueba si el narrador sabe lo que piensa su hermana.

origin.text: I opened the letter slowly, afraid of what it might say. In the next room my sister was singing, and I could not tell whether she had already read it.

prompt.es: Completa: «Este es un narrador limitado, no omnisciente.»

feedback.es: Un narrador que sigue una sola mente y no entra en la de los demás es limitado.

hint.es: Es el adjetivo contrario a omniscient: solo se abre una mente.

origin.text: We only ever see the story through Mara's eyes, and we never learn what her brother feels. This is a ___ narrator, not an omniscient one.

prompt.es: Ordena: «El narrador está al tanto de los pensamientos de cada personaje.»

answer.text: The narrator is privy to every character's thoughts

feedback.es: Be privy to va seguido de lo que el narrador conoce; every character's thoughts cierra la frase.

hint.es: Empieza por el sujeto y sigue con is privy to.

prompt.es: Escucha el relato y elige qué sabemos del hermano de quien narra.

choices.text: What he privately thinks about the letter, as the narrator explains.
Only his teasing, since the narrator cannot know what he thinks.
That he also received a letter from the grandfather years before.

feedback.es: El narrador solo cuenta cómo lo molestaba su hermano; no puede saber qué piensa, porque cuenta desde su propia mente.

origin.audio: When I was twelve, my grandfather handed me a letter and made me promise not to open it until I was older. I carried it for years, and whenever I touched the envelope my hands would tremble. My brother teased me about it constantly, but I never told him what I suspected: that the letter was not a goodbye at all, but an apology. I still wonder whether I was right.

prompt.es: Escucha otra vez y elige qué da a entender quien narra sobre la carta.

choices.text: That it is certainly an apology, as the grandfather had hinted.
That the narrator regrets having kept the promise to the grandfather.
That it may hold an apology, although nobody has confirmed it.

feedback.es: Quien narra sospecha que era una disculpa, pero termina con «I still wonder»: es una sospecha sin confirmar.

origin.audio: When I was twelve, my grandfather handed me a letter and made me promise not to open it until I was older. I carried it for years, and whenever I touched the envelope my hands would tremble. My brother teased me about it constantly, but I never told him what I suspected: that the letter was not a goodbye at all, but an apology. I still wonder whether I was right.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada fragmento con su tipo de narrador.

pairs: I never told anyone how afraid I was that evening.
We argued all night, and none of us dared to say what we feared.
She checked the map again, wondering if Leo had lied.
Mara feared the answer, while her father rehearsed his excuse.

feedback.es: El pronombre (I, we, she) y el número de mentes que se abren distinguen cada tipo de narrador.

pairs: I never told anyone how afraid I was that evening.
We argued all night, and none of us dared to say what we feared.
She checked the map again, wondering if Leo had lied.
Mara feared the answer, while her father rehearsed his excuse.

prompt.es: Escucha el fragmento y elige qué muestra que el narrador es omnisciente.

choices.text: The narrator reports the father's secret plans while Mara knows nothing about them.
The narrator uses the pronoun she, which always marks an omniscient voice.
The narrator describes the rain and the window from far away, like a camera.

feedback.es: El narrador cuenta lo que el padre planea en secreto mientras Mara lo ignora: entra en dos mentes a la vez.

origin.audio: The rain had not stopped all week. Mara sat by the window, convinced that her father had forgotten her birthday. Across town, he was wrapping the gift he had hidden for months, rehearsing what he would say. Neither of them suspected that the other was thinking about the same old photo, taken years before the argument.

prompt.es: Escucha otra vez y elige qué efecto consigue el narrador al abrir dos mentes.

choices.text: The reader learns that the father is lying to his daughter about the gift.
The reader sees a misunderstanding that neither character can see.
The reader expects Mara to forgive her father without any help.

feedback.es: Solo el lector sabe que ambos piensan en la misma foto y que el padre no la ha olvidado: ve lo que ellos no ven.

origin.audio: The rain had not stopped all week. Mara sat by the window, convinced that her father had forgotten her birthday. Across town, he was wrapping the gift he had hidden for months, rehearsing what he would say. Neither of them suspected that the other was thinking about the same old photo, taken years before the argument.

prompt.es: Completa: «…los críticos llaman al narrador poco fiable.»

feedback.es: Cuando el relato de quien cuenta choca con los hechos, se le llama narrador poco fiable (unreliable).

origin.text: He insists that he was at home all evening, yet everyone remembers seeing him at the harbour, so critics call the narrator ___.

prompt.es: Lee el fragmento. ¿Qué actitud transmite la voz del narrador hacia el comité?

choices.text: Warm respect: he praises how carefully each member weighs the question.
Open anger: he blames Mr Hale personally for wasting the morning.
Ironic distance: he watches the meeting with quiet humour.

feedback.es: «As committees do» y «to decide nothing» muestran una distancia irónica: observa con humor, sin implicarse; no hay respeto ni enojo.

origin.text: The committee met, as committees do, to decide nothing. Mr Hale spoke for an hour; the others nodded, looked at their watches and thought about lunch. By noon the agenda had been approved, and the real problem had, naturally, been left for next week.

prompt.es: Lee el texto. ¿Qué indica que el narrador solo sigue a Tom?

choices.text: We learn Tom's fears, but Ana's reaction stays unknown.
The narrator hints that Ana will forgive him, which Tom cannot yet see.
The story is told in the past tense, which always signals a limited narrator.

feedback.es: El lector conoce los miedos de Tom, pero no puede saber lo que siente Ana tras la puerta: hay una sola mente abierta.

origin.text: Tom waited outside the door, rehearsing his apology. Surely Ana would never forgive him; he had ruined everything. He called her name twice, but he could not tell whether the silence meant anger or sleep.

prompt.es: Completa: «Al omitir lo que quiere ocultar, puede engañar al lector sobre lo ocurrido.»

feedback.es: Mislead significa engañar o inducir a error: lo que el narrador calla puede desviar al lector.

origin.text: Notice what the narrator refuses to mention. By leaving out exactly what he wants to hide, he can ___ the reader about what really happened.

prompt.es: Escucha el comentario y elige qué sugiere sobre el narrador.

choices.text: That he is an omniscient observer with access to every mind.
That he knows more than he admits, so he may not be honest.
That he is honest but tends to exaggerate small details.

feedback.es: Conoce demasiados detalles para alguien que apenas conocía a la víctima: el lector duda de él, como ante un narrador poco fiable.

origin.audio: Our narrator insists that he hardly knew the man, yet he describes the man's habits, his money problems and even his favourite chair in great detail. He claims to be only curious, but the reader begins to wonder.

es: Reconocer el estilo indirecto libre y separar la voz del narrador de los pensamientos del personaje.

teaching.en: Free indirect style lets a narrator slip into a character's head without warning: Mara looked at the clock, and then came the question, was he really going to be late again?
teaching.es: El estilo indirecto libre permite que el narrador se deslice hacia la cabeza del personaje sin aviso: Mara miró el reloj y entonces llegó la pregunta: ¿de verdad iba a llegar tarde otra vez?
teaching.explanationEs: La pregunta directa dentro de la narración en pasado es la voz de Mara: no hay «she asked herself».
segments: Free indirect style lets a narrator slip into a character's head without warning: Mara looked at
the clock, and then came the question, was he really going to be late again?
teaching.audioText: Free indirect style lets a narrator slip into a character's head without warning: Mara looked at the clock, and then came the question, was he really going to be late again?

teaching.en: He would surely come tomorrow. Of course he would! The narrator never writes that she thought it, yet her certainty comes through clearly.
teaching.es: Seguro que vendría mañana. ¡Claro que vendría! El narrador nunca escribe que ella lo pensó, pero su certeza se oye con claridad.
teaching.explanationEs: Tomorrow en un relato en pasado es marca de estilo libre: el narrador diría the next day.
segments: He would surely come tomorrow. Of course he would! The narrator never
writes that she thought it, yet her certainty comes through clearly.
teaching.audioText: He would surely come tomorrow. Of course he would! The narrator never writes that she thought it, yet her certainty comes through clearly.

teaching.en: What a silly idea this was! The exclamation and the word this are subtle signals of her reaction, more direct than any reporting verb such as thought or wondered.
teaching.es: ¡Qué idea tan tonta era esta! La exclamación y la palabra this son señales sutiles de su reacción, más directas que cualquier verbo de transmisión como thought o wondered.
teaching.explanationEs: What a + exclamación es la voz de ella; this (y no that) acerca el texto a su mente; reporting verb = said, thought, wondered…
segments: What a silly idea this was! The exclamation and the word this are subtle signals
of her reaction, more direct than any reporting verb such as thought or wondered.
teaching.audioText: What a silly idea this was! The exclamation and the word this are subtle signals of her reaction, more direct than any reporting verb such as thought or wondered.

teaching.en: She had no doubt about it: he was coming, and nothing could stop him now. The word now belongs to her present, not to the narrator's past.
teaching.es: No tenía ninguna duda: él venía y nada podía detenerlo ahora. La palabra now pertenece al presente de ella, no al pasado del narrador.
teaching.explanationEs: Now dentro de un relato en pasado muestra el punto de vista del personaje, no el del narrador.
segments: She had no doubt about it: he was coming, and nothing could stop him
now. The word now belongs to her present, not to the narrator's past.
teaching.audioText: She had no doubt about it: he was coming, and nothing could stop him now. The word now belongs to her present, not to the narrator's past.

teaching.en: Mara felt nervous, and her mind went back to that day. Was it really her fault? The shift from narration to question is almost invisible.
teaching.es: Mara se sentía nerviosa y su mente volvió a aquel día. ¿De verdad era culpa suya? El paso de la narración a la pregunta casi no se nota.
teaching.explanationEs: Primero narración (felt nervous) y luego pensamiento en forma de pregunta directa, en pasado.
segments: Mara felt nervous, and her mind went back to that day. Was it
really her fault? The shift from narration to question is almost invisible.
teaching.audioText: Mara felt nervous, and her mind went back to that day. Was it really her fault? The shift from narration to question is almost invisible.

teaching.en: Free indirect style can blur the line between narrator and character, so you must decide whose thoughts you are reading before you attribute an opinion to either.
teaching.es: El estilo indirecto libre puede difuminar la frontera entre narrador y personaje, así que debes decidir de quién son los pensamientos antes de atribuir una opinión a uno u otro.
teaching.explanationEs: Blur = difuminar: cuando no se separan las voces, pregúntate quién habla.
segments: Free indirect style can blur the line between narrator and character, so you must
decide whose thoughts you are reading before you attribute an opinion to either.
teaching.audioText: Free indirect style can blur the line between narrator and character, so you must decide whose thoughts you are reading before you attribute an opinion to either.

prompt.es: Lee el fragmento. ¿Qué frase reproduce directamente el pensamiento de Mara?

choices.text: Mara looked at the clock and sighed.
Was he really going to be late again?
She walked to the door.

feedback.es: La pregunta directa, sin verbo de pensar, es la voz de Mara; las otras dos frases son narración.

hint.es: Busca la frase que pregunta algo directamente, sin she thought.

origin.text: Mara looked at the clock and sighed. Was he really going to be late again? She walked to the door.

prompt.es: Completa: «¿De verdad iba a llegar tarde otra vez?»

feedback.es: Se mantiene el pasado del narrador y se invierte el orden de la pregunta directa: Was he…?

hint.es: Pregunta directa en pasado: el verbo be va antes del sujeto.

origin.text: Mara stared at the clock. There was no she wondered, only her own voice in the paragraph: ___ he really going to be late again?

prompt.es: Ordena: «¡Qué idea tan tonta era esta!»

answer.text: What a silly idea this was

feedback.es: La exclamación What a + adjetivo + nombre mantiene el pasado (was) y deja oír la voz del personaje.

hint.es: Empieza por la exclamación: What a…

prompt.es: Escucha el relato y elige la frase que recoge un pensamiento de Tom.

choices.text: Tom stopped at the gate.
His heart was beating fast.
Surely Ana had forgotten him by now.

feedback.es: «Surely» y la duda sobre Ana no los dice el narrador: son la voz de Tom. Las otras dos frases solo narran hechos.

origin.audio: Tom stopped at the gate. Nothing moved in the house, except for a light upstairs. What a silly idea this was! Surely Ana had forgotten him by now. He would simply leave the flowers on the step and go home, and tomorrow nobody would even remember. Yet his heart was beating fast, and he could not make himself turn away. Was that really all he wanted?

prompt.es: Escucha otra vez y elige qué revela la última pregunta del fragmento.

choices.text: That Tom doubts his own plan and suspects he wants more.
That the narrator is asking the reader what Tom should do.
That Tom is sure that leaving the flowers is enough.

feedback.es: La pregunta sin verbo de pensar es la voz de Tom: duda de que dejar las flores sea todo lo que quiere.

origin.audio: Tom stopped at the gate. Nothing moved in the house, except for a light upstairs. What a silly idea this was! Surely Ana had forgotten him by now. He would simply leave the flowers on the step and go home, and tomorrow nobody would even remember. Yet his heart was beating fast, and he could not make himself turn away. Was that really all he wanted?

prompt.es: Relaciona cada frase con el tipo de discurso que emplea.

pairs: Mara thought that he would be late.

pairs.es: estilo indirecto, con verbo de pensar

pairs: He would be late again!
Mara looked at the clock.
'He will be late again,' she thought.

feedback.es: El verbo de transmisión, las comillas o su ausencia permiten separar narración, discurso indirecto, libre y directo.

pairs: Mara thought that he would be late.

pairs.es: estilo indirecto, con verbo de pensar

pairs: He would be late again!
Mara looked at the clock.
'He will be late again,' she thought.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué aporta «tomorrow Ana would…» a la escena.

choices.text: It announces what the narrator will describe in the next chapter.
It lets us hear Leo imagining the consequences in his own words.
It reports a decision that Ana made before the train left.

feedback.es: Tomorrow dentro de un relato en pasado mira el futuro desde el presente de Leo: deja oír cómo imagina las consecuencias, no un anuncio del narrador.

origin.audio: Leo watched the train pull out. Why had he not waited? Now everything was ruined, and tomorrow Ana would not even look at him. The platform was nearly empty, and the only sound was the clock above it.

prompt.es: Escucha otra vez y elige qué efecto logra la última frase sobre el andén.

choices.text: It suggests that the narrator finds Leo's regret rather exaggerated.
It hints that Leo has decided to wait for the next train.
It shows how alone Leo feels without naming the feeling.

feedback.es: El andén casi vacío y el único sonido del reloj reflejan la soledad de Leo sin decir «he felt lonely»: el ánimo se sugiere.

origin.audio: Leo watched the train pull out. Why had he not waited? Now everything was ruined, and tomorrow Ana would not even look at him. The platform was nearly empty, and the only sound was the clock above it.

prompt.es: Completa: «La pregunta es una señal sutil de su preocupación.»

feedback.es: Subtle significa sutil: el estilo libre deja la emoción en una señal que el lector debe notar.

origin.text: The writer never says that she is anxious. The question is a ___ signal of her worry, and the reader has to notice it.

prompt.es: Elige la versión en estilo indirecto libre del pensamiento de Sara.

choices.text: Her brother would surely forget the tickets again. Of course he would!
Her brother will surely forget the tickets again. Of course he will!
Sara thought that surely her brother would forget the tickets again.

feedback.es: El estilo libre mantiene el pasado (would), usa exclamación y no lleva verbo de pensar; will lo cambiaría a presente.

origin.text: The story is told in the past tense. Sara's brother always forgot things, and the narrator lets us hear her thoughts without any reporting verb.

prompt.es: Lee el texto. ¿Qué da a entender la última frase sobre la actitud de Carlos?

choices.text: That he has accepted failure and no longer cares about the exam.
That he watches his own panic with a certain ironic distance.
That he enjoys exams because they make him feel more alive.

feedback.es: Comparar su desastre con «a story about somebody else» muestra que lo mira con cierta distancia irónica.

origin.text: Carlos stared at the clock. The exam was tomorrow, and he knew nothing. Surely somebody had notes! He felt nervous, yet part of him almost enjoyed the panic, as if the disaster were only a story about somebody else.

prompt.es: Completa: «…puede difuminar la frontera entre narrador y personaje.»

feedback.es: Blur the line es la colocación para borrar la frontera entre dos cosas, aquí narrador y personaje.

origin.text: Some texts are hard to classify, because free indirect style can ___ the line between the narrator's voice and the character's own.

prompt.es: Escucha el fragmento y elige qué sugiere la última frase sobre la protagonista.

choices.text: She is resigned to being the joke of the whole party.
She is curious to see how the joke will end.
She is determined not to let the others laugh at her.

feedback.es: «Well, she would not give them that chance» es la voz de ella: decide no dejar que se rían de ella.

origin.audio: She had no doubt about it: the letter was a joke. Now she saw the whole plan! Her sister had written it years ago, and tomorrow everyone at the party would laugh at her. Well, she would not give them that chance.

es: Comprender el estado de ánimo, el motivo y una expresión clave de un personaje a partir de sus acciones en un fragmento de cuento (texto y audio).

teaching.en: Mara feels anxious before the exam, so she tries to avoid her friends, and by the evening she has come to dread every conversation about results.
teaching.es: Mara se siente inquieta antes del examen, así que intenta evitar a sus amigos, y por la tarde ya teme cualquier conversación sobre las notas.
teaching.explanationEs: El ánimo (anxious) explica la acción (avoid) y dread nombra el miedo a lo que viene: del motivo a la conducta.
segments: Mara feels anxious before the exam, so she tries to avoid her friends,
and by the evening she has come to dread every conversation about results.
teaching.audioText: Mara feels anxious before the exam, so she tries to avoid her friends, and by the evening she has come to dread every conversation about results.

teaching.en: Leo is eager to start the project, but his sister looks reluctant, probably because she cannot forget how badly the last one ended.
teaching.es: Leo tiene muchas ganas de empezar el proyecto, pero su hermana parece reacia, probablemente porque no olvida lo mal que acabó el último.
teaching.explanationEs: Eager y reluctant son opuestos: muchas ganas frente a poca gana de hacer algo, y el texto suele dar la razón.
segments: Leo is eager to start the project, but his sister looks reluctant,
probably because she cannot forget how badly the last one ended.
teaching.audioText: Leo is eager to start the project, but his sister looks reluctant, probably because she cannot forget how badly the last one ended.

teaching.en: When the door finally opened, Tom felt relieved: nobody had seen him, and he could brush off the teasing that would certainly follow.
teaching.es: Cuando por fin se abrió la puerta, Tom se sintió aliviado: nadie lo había visto y podría quitar importancia a las burlas que seguramente vendrían.
teaching.explanationEs: Relieved es el ánimo de quien deja de preocuparse; had seen sitúa el hecho antes del alivio y brush off es restar importancia.
segments: When the door finally opened, Tom felt relieved: nobody had seen him,
and he could brush off the teasing that would certainly follow.
teaching.audioText: When the door finally opened, Tom felt relieved: nobody had seen him, and he could brush off the teasing that would certainly follow.

teaching.en: She felt guilty because she had not called her grandmother, and the longer she waited, the more sheepish she felt about picking up the phone.
teaching.es: Se sentía culpable porque no había llamado a su abuela, y cuanto más esperaba, más cohibida se sentía para contestar el teléfono.
teaching.explanationEs: Guilty + because da el motivo de la emoción con un hecho anterior (had not called); sheepish añade vergüenza.
segments: She felt guilty because she had not called her grandmother, and the longer
she waited, the more sheepish she felt about picking up the phone.
teaching.audioText: She felt guilty because she had not called her grandmother, and the longer she waited, the more sheepish she felt about picking up the phone.

teaching.en: He began to hesitate at the door, and his real motive, which he never admitted to anyone, was to say sorry.
teaching.es: Empezó a dudar ante la puerta, y su verdadero motivo, que nunca admitió ante nadie, era pedir perdón.
teaching.explanationEs: Hesitate es una acción que muestra el ánimo; motive es la razón que explica lo que hace.
segments: He began to hesitate at the door, and his real motive,
which he never admitted to anyone, was to say sorry.
teaching.audioText: He began to hesitate at the door, and his real motive, which he never admitted to anyone, was to say sorry.

teaching.en: She did not speak; she only continued to stare at the old photo, and that silence told the reader more than any adjective could have done.
teaching.es: No habló; solo siguió mirando fijamente la vieja foto, y ese silencio dijo al lector más de lo que habría dicho cualquier adjetivo.
teaching.explanationEs: Stare at es una acción sin palabras: el autor muestra el ánimo sin nombrarlo.
segments: She did not speak; she only continued to stare at the old photo,
and that silence told the reader more than any adjective could have done.
teaching.audioText: She did not speak; she only continued to stare at the old photo, and that silence told the reader more than any adjective could have done.

prompt.es: Lee el texto. ¿Qué explica mejor la conducta de Mara?

choices.text: She is eager to spend the week alone with her own thoughts.
She is relieved that her friends have finally stopped calling.
She is anxious about something she does not want to discuss.

feedback.es: Evitar a los amigos y contestar con una palabra sugiere inquietud ante algo que no quiere tratar, no ganas de estar sola.

hint.es: Fíjate en las acciones: ¿qué ánimo y qué motivo encajan con ellas?

origin.text: Mara has been avoiding her friends all week. She leaves the library when they come in, and she answers their messages with one word, if she answers at all.

prompt.es: Completa: «Tom se sintió aliviado cuando se abrió la puerta.»

feedback.es: Relieved es el ánimo de quien deja de preocuparse al comprobar que no pasó lo temido.

prompt.es: Escribe la escena de recuerdo que se pide en el recuadro.

answer.text: I remember standing on my grandmother's porch on hot summer evenings, when the air was warm and heavy and the scent of fresh bread drifted out of the kitchen. I can still hear the creak of the old gate and the echo of my cousins laughing in the garden. I will never forget watching the sun go down behind the hills while she told us stories about her own childhood. One evening I forgot to say goodbye when my parents took me home, and I still regret not hugging her that night. When I look back on those summers, I realise how much they shaped me. Now I must remember to call her every Sunday, because the scent of bread alone is not enough to keep a voice alive. Some memories linger for ever, small and golden, exactly as they were.
accepted: I remember standing on my grandmother's porch on hot summer evenings, when the air was warm and heavy and the scent of fresh bread drifted out of the kitchen. I can still hear the creak of the old gate and the echo of my cousins laughing in the garden. I will never forget watching the sun go down behind the hills while she told us stories about her own childhood. One evening I forgot to say goodbye when my parents took me home, and I still regret not hugging her that night. When I look back on those summers, I realise how much they shaped me. Now I must remember to call her every Sunday, because the scent of bread alone is not enough to keep a voice alive. Some memories linger for ever, small and golden, exactly as they were.

I remember playing in my grandfather's garden every summer, long before I understood how rare those days were. The air was warm, and the scent of ripe apples was everywhere. I can still hear the creak of the wooden gate and the echo of his voice calling us in for dinner. I will never forget eating under the big tree while he told funny stories about his youth. I regret not asking him more questions about his life, and I must remember to visit his house again this year. When I look back on those evenings, I realise that the smallest details are the ones that stay with me. Even now, when I close my eyes, that garden comes back, small and green and full of light. It is a vivid memory, and I do not want to forget it.

A scene that reminded her of her own experience.
The faster pacing of the final chapters.

feedback.es: La escena de la carta le recordó la espera de noticias de su abuela: fue una conexión personal, no una reseña ni el ritmo.

origin.audio: Honestly, I was not sure about the book at first. The first chapters are slow, and I nearly gave up. But the letter scene changed everything for me: I suddenly remembered waiting for news from my own grandmother, and I could not put the book down after that.

prompt.es: Escucha otra vez y elige con qué propósito cuenta su recuerdo personal.

choices.text: To show why the slow chapters should have been cut.
To persuade the club to read another book about letters.
To explain why the book finally won her over.

feedback.es: Cuenta el recuerdo para justificar por qué el libro terminó convenciéndola después de un comienzo lento.

feedback.es: Take issue with es la fórmula para discrepar con tacto de una afirmación concreta, y aquí la apoya un dato del capítulo.

origin.text: Much as I like your reading, Tom, I must ___ issue with your claim that the characters are flat: Mara changes completely in chapter three.

prompt.es: Escribe tu intervención en el club de lectura: resumen, recuerdo y respuesta.

answer.text: Thanks, Tom. I see your point, but I would take issue with the claim that the ending was rushed. In chapter six, the plot turns when Mara finds her grandmother's old letter hidden in an old book, and the pacing slows so that we can feel her hesitation. Although the final pages are quiet, I found them very moving. I can relate to Mara, because I remember waiting for a letter from my own grandmother every summer. I will never forget opening the envelope and seeing her small, careful handwriting. That memory made the last scene feel true to me, and it is bound to strike a chord with anyone who has waited for news. Perhaps the ending is not exciting, but it is honest. I also regret not keeping her letters, which may be why the chapter reminds me of her so strongly. What do the rest of you think?

I understand your point, Tom, but I do not agree that the ending was rushed, and I would take issue with calling it boring. In this chapter, the plot changes when Mara finds a letter in her aunt's kitchen and decides to read it in secret, and the pacing slows to show how nervous she is. Though the last scene is slow, I thought it was gripping. I can relate to Mara, because I remember writing letters to my cousin every summer when I was a child. I will never forget waiting by the gate for his reply, and that memory reminds me how important small moments can be. It is bound to strike a chord with many readers, even if the ending is not exciting. I regret not finishing the book earlier, because I would love to discuss it with the whole club. Does anyone else feel the same way?

feedback.es: Una buena intervención resume el capítulo, conecta con un recuerdo vivido y responde con cortesía a la otra opinión.

origin.text: Tom dice: «I think the ending was rushed and boring.» Escribe tu intervención en inglés (entre 150 y 250 palabras): resume un capítulo de «A Letter for Mara» (Mara encuentra una carta vieja), cuenta un recuerdo con remember + -ing y responde con cortesía a Tom usando I see your point y although.

prompt.es: Lee la nota. ¿Qué postura final adopta quien escribe sobre el libro?

choices.text: Positive overall, with a reservation about the pacing.
Negative overall, with a few polite words of praise.
Cautiously negative: she recommends it only when somebody insists.

feedback.es: Esperaba no gustarle, acabó conmovida y lo recomienda, con una advertencia sobre el comienzo lento.

origin.text: I'll be honest: I expected to dislike it. The plot sounds slight, and the pacing is slow in the middle. Yet by the last chapter I was quietly moved, and I have recommended it ever since, although always with a warning about the slow start.

prompt.es: Completa: «Las últimas páginas fueron tan absorbentes que las leí de una sentada.»

feedback.es: Gripping describe un pasaje que atrapa tanto que no puedes dejar de leer; aquí el contexto pide un adjetivo de intensidad.

origin.text: The middle chapters were rather slow, but the last fifty pages were so ___ that I finished them in one sitting.

prompt.es: Escucha el comentario y elige qué sugiere «even so» en las palabras de Carlos.

choices.text: That he agrees with the members who find the novel overrated.
That its lasting effect outweighs his doubts about the pacing.
That he would recommend it only to people who like slow books.

feedback.es: Even so introduce el contraste: pese a que el ritmo le pareció lento, el efecto duradero del libro pesa más.

origin.audio: Some members argued that the novel is overrated, and Carlos admitted that he found the middle slow. Even so, he said he would recommend it, because it makes you think about your own family long after you have finished the last page.
